B-cell neoplasms (85-90%): diffuse large B-cell (DLBCL, the commonest, about a third), follicular, CLL/SLL, mantle cell, marginal zone/MALT, Burkitt, lymphoplasmacytic, hairy cell leukaemia, plasma cell myeloma.

High-grade NHL: The most common form, diffuse large B-cell
NHL, responds to cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine,
prednisolone, and rituximab (R-CHOP).
Mature B-cell lymphomas comprise 2 main pathologies, Burkitt lymphoma (BL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

qs.q: A 32-year-old man has 2 months of worsening headaches. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. CBC: Hgb 12, platelets 250,000, WBC 6000 with 80% granulocytes and 10% lymphocytes. Head CT shows a 3 cm mass next to the right lateral ventricle. Biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Most likely lab finding?
qs.e: Primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in a 32-year-old with relative lymphopenia = AIDS-related lymphoma. HIV infection is the most important risk factor. HIV-1 RNA viral load would be detectable, reflecting underlying HIV infection driving the lymphoma.

es.q: For Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL), state the standard chemotherapy regimen. Additionally, name two monoclonal antibodies used in NHL treatment and specify their respective targets.
es.m: 1. **DLBCL Standard Regimen:** R-CHOP (Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin (Vincristine), Prednisolone). 2. **Monoclonal Antibodies and Targets:** * **Rituximab:** Targets CD20 (used for B-cell NHL). * **Brentuximab:** Targets CD30 (used for Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma - ALCL).

es.q: A 45-year-old patient is diagnosed with Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). What is the standard first-line chemotherapy regimen for this subtype, and what specific type of monoclonal antibody is typically included in this regimen, based on the article?
es.m: The standard first-line chemotherapy regimen for DLBCL is R-CHOP. This regimen includes Rituximab, which is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, targeting the CD20 antigen found on B-cells.

first: DLBCL: R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone)
Burkitt: intensive cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and high-dose methotrexate with folinic rescue, plus intrathecal therapy

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common aggressive non‑Hodgkin lymphoma, presenting as rapidly enlarging masses that may involve lymph nodes or extranodal sites. Diagnosis relies on histology, immunophenotype and staging. Treatment combines rituximab with CHOP chemotherapy, with prognosis depending on stage and IPI score.

sections.p: DLBCL is a malignant proliferation of large B‑cells that form sheets on histology. It is diagnosed by biopsy showing large atypical lymphocytes, CD20 positivity, and exclusion of other lymphoma subtypes.

t.b: Shows sheets of large atypical B‑cells; confirms DLBCL
Defines cell of origin (germinal center vs activated B‑cell) and guides prognosis

t.a: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for MYC, BCL2, BCL6
t.b: Detects double/triple hit status, indicating poorer outcome

sections.p: Staging follows the Ann Arbor system with IPI risk stratification. Stage I–IV reflects nodal involvement; extranodal disease and bulky masses raise IPI points.
b: IPI score: age, LDH, performance status, stage, extranodal sites

t.b: Defines extent of nodal and extranodal disease; used for staging and response assessment
Elevated LDH correlates with tumor burden and poorer prognosis

sections.p: DLBCL arises de novo or from transformation of indolent B‑cell lymphomas. Risk factors include immunosuppression, HIV, hepatitis B, and chronic inflammation.

t.b: Identifies immunosuppressed patients who may need rituximab‑based therapy with caution
Screen for hepatitis B reactivation risk before rituximab

sections.p: Patients often have rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, weight loss, or extranodal symptoms such as abdominal pain, CNS deficits, or skin lesions.
b: B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)

t.b: Detects size, consistency, and tenderness of nodes; assesses CNS signs if brain involvement

sections.p: Work‑up includes imaging, laboratory tests, and biopsy. In low‑resource settings, basic imaging and histology may suffice.

t.b: Anemia, leukocytosis, or thrombocytopenia may indicate marrow involvement
High levels suggest high tumor turnover and poorer prognosis
Assesses nodal and extranodal disease when PET is unavailable

sections.p: Rapidly enlarging nodes, CNS symptoms, severe B symptoms, or organ dysfunction signal aggressive disease or impending complications.

t.b: Detects focal deficits indicating CNS lymphoma
Assesses marrow infiltration and guides staging

sections.p: First‑line therapy is rituximab plus CHOP chemotherapy. Supportive care includes infection prophylaxis and monitoring for tumor lysis syndrome.

t.b: Targets CD20 on B‑cells; improves survival
Cytotoxic regimen effective against rapidly dividing cells

sections.p: Patients are monitored with periodic imaging and labs. Prevention focuses on early detection of indolent lymphomas and managing HIV/HBV to reduce transformation risk.
DLBCL can mimic other aggressive lymphomas, metastatic carcinoma, or infectious lymphadenitis.
Low‑grade or early disease may show normal LDH; small biopsies can miss focal involvement; HIV serology may be false negative early.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging lymph node >2 cm in 2 weeks

faq.q: Can DLBCL arise from a normal lymph node?
faq.a: Yes, it can develop de novo without prior lymphoma.

faq.q: Is rituximab safe in HIV patients?
faq.a: Yes, but monitor for infections and consider HBV reactivation.

faq.q: What if PET scan is unavailable?
faq.a: Use CT or MRI and clinical staging; consider bone marrow biopsy for accurate staging.
